name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_DIAGRAM_Q01 - Zinc rod in aqueous copper nitrate

questiontext.text:
The diagram below illustrates the progression of a redox reaction when a zinc rod is placed in an aqueous copper(II) nitrate solution.

Which of the following correctly identifies the species oxidised, the species reduced, and the reason for the disappearance of the blue colour?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows three stages of immersing a metallic zinc (\(\mathrm{Zn}\)) rod into an aqueous blue solution of copper(II) nitrate (\(\mathrm{Cu(NO_3)_2}\)). Over time, the blue colour fades to colourless and a reddish-brown metallic deposit forms on the submerged portion of the zinc rod.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In aqueous solution, copper(II) nitrate dissociates to give hydrated \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) ions, which impart the characteristic blue colour. Oxidation corresponds to loss of electrons (increase in oxidation number), and reduction corresponds to gain of electrons (decrease in oxidation number).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The net ionic equation for the competitive electron transfer between zinc and copper(II) ions is:
\[\mathrm{Zn(s)} + \mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq)} + \mathrm{Cu(s)}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Metallic \(\mathrm{Zn(s)}\) (oxidation number \(0\)) loses two electrons to form colourless \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq)}\) ions (oxidation number \(+2\)): \(\mathrm{Zn(s)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^-}\). Thus, \(\mathrm{Zn}\) is oxidised.
2. Aqueous \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)}\) ions (oxidation number \(+2\)) gain two electrons to deposit as reddish-brown metallic \(\mathrm{Cu(s)}\) (oxidation number \(0\)): \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu(s)}\). Thus, \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) is reduced.
3. As \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)}\) ions are progressively consumed and replaced by colourless \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq)}\) ions, the blue colour of the solution disappears.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Mass and charge are balanced in the net ionic equation, and the visual observations match the conversion of blue \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) to solid \(\mathrm{Cu}\). Therefore, \(\mathrm{Zn}\) is oxidised to \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\), \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) is reduced to \(\mathrm{Cu}\), and the blue colour disappears due to the consumption of \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) ions.

answer.text: \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) is oxidised to \(\mathrm{Cu}\); \(\mathrm{Zn}\) is reduced to \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\); blue colour disappears due to formation of \(\mathrm{ZnS}\).
\(\mathrm{Zn}\) is oxidised to \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\); \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) is reduced to \(\mathrm{Cu}\); blue colour disappears due to consumption of \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) ions.
\(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) is oxidised to \(\mathrm{Zn}\); \(\mathrm{Cu}\) is reduced to \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\); blue colour disappears due to precipitation of \(\mathrm{Cu(NO_3)_2}\).
\(\mathrm{NO_3^-}\) is oxidised to \(\mathrm{NO_2}\); \(\mathrm{Zn}\) is reduced to \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\); blue colour disappears due to formation of \(\mathrm{NH_3}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_DIAGRAM_Q02 - Electron transfer in sodium sulphide formation

questiontext.text: Based on the electron-transfer schematic shown below for the formation of sodium sulphide, identify Process X, Process Y, and the oxidising agent in this reaction.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The schematic represents the reaction \(2\mathrm{Na(s)} + \mathrm{S(s)} \rightarrow (\mathrm{Na^+})_2\mathrm{S^{2-}(s)}\). Process X connects \(2\mathrm{Na(s)}\) to \((\mathrm{Na^+})_2\), and Process Y connects \(\mathrm{S(s)}\) to \(\mathrm{S^{2-}}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Sodium sulphide is an ionic compound composed of \(\mathrm{Na^+}\) cations and \(\mathrm{S^{2-}}\) anions. In electronic terms, oxidation is the loss of electrons, reduction is the gain of electrons, and an oxidising agent is an electron acceptor.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Oxidation half-reaction: \(2\mathrm{Na(s)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Na^+} + 2\mathrm{e^-}\)
Reduction half-reaction: \(\mathrm{S(s)} + 2\mathrm{e^-} \rightarrow \mathrm{S^{2-}}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. In Process X, two neutral sodium atoms each lose one electron (a total loss of \(2\mathrm{e^-}\)) to form \(2\mathrm{Na^+}\) ions. Loss of electrons is oxidation.
2. In Process Y, one neutral sulphur atom gains two electrons (gain of \(2\mathrm{e^-}\)) to form the \(\mathrm{S^{2-}}\) ion. Gain of electrons is reduction.
3. Because \(\mathrm{S(s)}\) accepts electrons from sodium, \(\mathrm{S(s)}\) acts as the oxidising agent.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The total electrons lost in Process X (\(2\mathrm{e^-}\)) equal the total electrons gained in Process Y (\(2\mathrm{e^-}\)). Therefore, Process X is the loss of \(2\mathrm{e^-}\) (oxidation), Process Y is the gain of \(2\mathrm{e^-}\) (reduction), and \(\mathrm{S(s)}\) is the oxidising agent.

answer.text: Process X: loss of \(2\mathrm{e^-}\) (oxidation); Process Y: gain of \(2\mathrm{e^-}\) (reduction); Oxidising agent: \(\mathrm{S(s)}\)
Process X: gain of \(2\mathrm{e^-}\) (reduction); Process Y: loss of \(2\mathrm{e^-}\) (oxidation); Oxidising agent: \(\mathrm{Na(s)}\)
Process X: loss of \(2\mathrm{e^-}\) (oxidation); Process Y: gain of \(2\mathrm{e^-}\) (reduction); Oxidising agent: \(\mathrm{Na(s)}\)
Process X: gain of \(2\mathrm{e^-}\) (oxidation); Process Y: loss of \(2\mathrm{e^-}\) (reduction); Oxidising agent: \(\mathrm{S^{2-}}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_DIAGRAM_Q03 - Copper rod in aqueous silver nitrate

questiontext.text:
The diagram below depicts a copper rod immersed in an aqueous \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\) solution over time.

What is the balanced ionic equation for the reaction occurring in the beaker, and which species acts as the reducing agent?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows a copper (\(\mathrm{Cu}\)) rod placed in an initially colourless aqueous solution of silver nitrate (\(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\)). As the reaction proceeds, the solution turns deep blue and a silvery-grey deposit forms on the copper rod.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The blue colour of the aqueous solution is due to the formation of \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)}\) ions, and the silvery deposit on the rod is metallic silver, \(\mathrm{Ag(s)}\). The reducing agent is the species that donates electrons and gets oxidised.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Oxidation half-reaction: \(\mathrm{Cu(s)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^-}\)
Reduction half-reaction: \(\mathrm{Ag^+(aq)} + \mathrm{e^-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ag(s)}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
To balance the electrons transferred, multiply the reduction half-reaction by \(2\):
\[2\mathrm{Ag^+(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^-} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Ag(s)}\]
Adding the two half-reactions and cancelling \(2\mathrm{e^-}\) on both sides gives:
\[\mathrm{Cu(s)} + 2\mathrm{Ag^+(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{Ag(s)}\]
Here, \(\mathrm{Cu(s)}\) loses electrons to reduce \(\mathrm{Ag^+(aq)}\) to \(\mathrm{Ag(s)}\), so \(\mathrm{Cu(s)}\) is the reducing agent.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Both atoms (\(1\text{ Cu}, 2\text{ Ag}\)) and net charge (\(+2\) on both sides) are balanced. Thus, the balanced ionic equation is \(\mathrm{Cu(s)} + 2\mathrm{Ag^+(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{Ag(s)}\), and the reducing agent is \(\mathrm{Cu(s)}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_DIAGRAM_Q04 - Operation and polarity of Daniell cell

questiontext.text:
In the Daniell cell schematic shown below, arrow P represents the movement of electrons from the left electrode to the right electrode when the switch is closed.

Which of the following statements is correct regarding the polarity of the electrodes, arrow Q, and the half-cell reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows a Daniell cell with a zinc (\(\mathrm{Zn}\)) electrode in aqueous \(\mathrm{ZnSO_4}\) on the left and a copper (\(\mathrm{Cu}\)) electrode in aqueous \(\mathrm{CuSO_4}\) on the right, connected by a salt bridge and an external wire with an ammeter. Arrow \(\mathrm{P}\) points from left to right (electron flow), and arrow \(\mathrm{Q}\) points from right to left.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In a galvanic cell, oxidation occurs at the anode (negative electrode, source of electrons) and reduction occurs at the cathode (positive electrode). By convention, electric current flows in the direction opposite to electron flow.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Anode half-reaction (oxidation): \(\mathrm{Zn(s)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^-}\)
Cathode half-reaction (reduction): \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu(s)}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Since electrons (arrow \(\mathrm{P}\)) flow from the left \(\mathrm{Zn}\) electrode to the right \(\mathrm{Cu}\) electrode, \(\mathrm{Zn}\) is oxidised to \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) at the left electrode. Thus, the left electrode is the anode and is negatively charged (\(-\)).
2. Electrons arriving at the right \(\mathrm{Cu}\) electrode reduce \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)}\) to \(\mathrm{Cu(s)}\). Thus, the right electrode is the cathode and is positively charged (\(+\)).
3. Arrow \(\mathrm{Q}\), pointing from the right electrode to the left electrode (opposite to electron flow), represents the direction of conventional electric current.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The electron flow, conventional current direction, electrode polarities, and oxidation half-reaction at the zinc anode are all mutually consistent. Therefore, the left electrode is the anode (\(-\)), arrow \(\mathrm{Q}\) represents conventional current flow, and \(\mathrm{Zn(s)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^-}\) occurs at the left electrode.

answer.text: Left electrode is cathode (\(+\)); arrow Q shows cation migration; reduction occurs at the \(\mathrm{Zn}\) rod.
Left electrode is anode (\(+\)); arrow Q shows conventional current flow; oxidation occurs at the \(\mathrm{Cu}\) rod.
Right electrode is cathode (\(-\)); arrow Q shows electron flow; \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) is oxidised at the right electrode.
Left electrode is anode (\(-\)); arrow Q shows conventional current flow; \(\mathrm{Zn(s)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^-}\) occurs at the left electrode.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_DIAGRAM_Q05 - Oxidation states in carbon suboxide structure

questiontext.text:
The structural formula of carbon suboxide (\(\mathrm{C_3O_2}\)) is shown below, with the three carbon atoms labeled \(\mathrm{C_1}\), \(\mathrm{C_2}\), and \(\mathrm{C_3}\).

What are the individual oxidation numbers of \(\mathrm{C_1}\), \(\mathrm{C_2}\), and \(\mathrm{C_3}\), respectively, and the average oxidation number of carbon in \(\mathrm{C_3O_2}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The structure of carbon suboxide is linear: \(\mathrm{O}=\mathrm{C_{(1)}}=\mathrm{C_{(2)}}=\mathrm{C_{(3)}}=\mathrm{O}\). Each terminal carbon (\(\mathrm{C_1}\) and \(\mathrm{C_3}\)) forms a double bond with an oxygen atom and a double bond with the central carbon (\(\mathrm{C_2}\)).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so each bond between carbon and oxygen shifts the shared electrons toward oxygen (giving \(+1\) per bond to carbon and \(-1\) per bond to oxygen). A bond between two identical carbon atoms contributes \(0\) to the oxidation number of each carbon.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Average oxidation number of carbon in neutral \(\mathrm{C_3O_2}\): \(3x + 2(-2) = 0\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. For terminal carbon \(\mathrm{C_1}\): It has two bonds to oxygen (\(+2\)) and two bonds to \(\mathrm{C_2}\) (\(0\)), so its oxidation number is \(+2\).
2. For central carbon \(\mathrm{C_2}\): It is bonded only to \(\mathrm{C_1}\) and \(\mathrm{C_3}\) (identical atoms), so its oxidation number is \(0\).
3. For terminal carbon \(\mathrm{C_3}\): By symmetry with \(\mathrm{C_1}\), it has two bonds to oxygen (\(+2\)) and two bonds to \(\mathrm{C_2}\) (\(0\)), so its oxidation number is \(+2\).
4. The average oxidation number of the three carbon atoms is:
\[\frac{(+2) + 0 + (+2)}{3} = +\frac{4}{3}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The sum of all oxidation numbers in \(\mathrm{C_3O_2}\) is \((-2) + (+2) + 0 + (+2) + (-2) = 0\), confirming neutrality. Thus, the individual oxidation numbers of \(\mathrm{C_1}\), \(\mathrm{C_2}\), and \(\mathrm{C_3}\) are \(+2, 0, +2\), and the average oxidation number is \(+\frac{4}{3}\).

questiontext.text: Based on the structure of tribromooctaoxide (\(\mathrm{Br_3O_8}\)) shown below, what are the oxidation numbers of each terminal bromine atom (\(\mathrm{Br_1}\) and \(\mathrm{Br_3}\)) and the central bromine atom (\(\mathrm{Br_2}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The structure of \(\mathrm{Br_3O_8}\) shows a chain of three bromine atoms (\(\mathrm{Br_1-Br_2-Br_3}\)). Each terminal bromine (\(\mathrm{Br_1}\) and \(\mathrm{Br_3}\)) is double-bonded to three oxygen atoms and single-bonded to \(\mathrm{Br_2}\). The central bromine (\(\mathrm{Br_2}\)) is double-bonded to two oxygen atoms and single-bonded to \(\mathrm{Br_1}\) and \(\mathrm{Br_3}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Oxygen is more electronegative than bromine, so each \(\mathrm{Br=O}\) double bond contributes \(+2\) to the oxidation state of bromine (and \(-2\) to oxygen). Each \(\mathrm{Br-Br}\) bond between identical atoms contributes \(0\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The oxidation number of an atom in a covalent structure is the sum of bond contributions based on electronegativity differences.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. For each terminal bromine (\(\mathrm{Br_1}\) and \(\mathrm{Br_3}\)): It forms three \(\mathrm{Br=O}\) double bonds (\(3 \times (+2) = +6\)) and one \(\mathrm{Br-Br}\) bond (\(0\)). Hence, the oxidation state of each terminal bromine is \(+6\).
2. For the central bromine (\(\mathrm{Br_2}\)): It forms two \(\mathrm{Br=O}\) double bonds (\(2 \times (+2) = +4\)) and two \(\mathrm{Br-Br}\) bonds (\(0\)). Hence, the oxidation state of the central bromine is \(+4\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking the total oxidation number: \((+6) + (+4) + (+6) + 8(-2) = +16 - 16 = 0\), and the average oxidation number is \(\frac{16}{3}\), matching the formula \(\mathrm{Br_3O_8}\). Therefore, each terminal bromine is in the \(+6\) oxidation state and the central bromine is in the \(+4\) oxidation state.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_DIAGRAM_Q07 - Standard electrode potential chart and reducing power

questiontext.text: Using the standard electrode potential (\(E^\circ\)) chart at \(298\text{ K}\) shown below, identify the correct increasing order of reducing power of the metals \(\mathrm{Ag, Cu, Zn, Mg, K}\), and determine which metal can displace \(\mathrm{H_2}\) from dilute acid and reduce \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) to \(\mathrm{Cu}\), yet has weaker reducing power than \(\mathrm{Mg}\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
From the bar chart at \(298\text{ K}\), the standard reduction potentials are:
\(E^\circ(\mathrm{K^+/K}) = -2.93\text{ V}\)
\(E^\circ(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}/Mg}) = -2.36\text{ V}\)
\(E^\circ(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}/Zn}) = -0.76\text{ V}\)
\(E^\circ(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}/Cu}) = +0.34\text{ V}\)
\(E^\circ(\mathrm{Ag^+/Ag}) = +0.80\text{ V}\)
Also, by convention, \(E^\circ(\mathrm{H^+/H_2}) = 0.00\text{ V}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
A more negative (lower) standard reduction potential \(E^\circ\) means a greater tendency for the reduced metal to lose electrons and act as a stronger reducing agent.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For a metal \(\mathrm{M}\) to displace \(\mathrm{H_2}\) from dilute acid and reduce \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) to \(\mathrm{Cu}\), its \(E^\circ\) must be lower than both \(0.00\text{ V}\) and \(+0.34\text{ V}\). To be a weaker reducing agent than \(\mathrm{Mg}\), its \(E^\circ\) must be higher than \(-2.36\text{ V}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Ordering the \(E^\circ\) values from highest (weakest reducing agent) to lowest (strongest reducing agent):
\[+0.80\text{ V} > +0.34\text{ V} > -0.76\text{ V} > -2.36\text{ V} > -2.93\text{ V}\]
This gives the increasing order of reducing power as \(\mathrm{Ag} < \mathrm{Cu} < \mathrm{Zn} < \mathrm{Mg} < \mathrm{K}\).
2. Checking the condition \(-2.36\text{ V} < E^\circ < 0.00\text{ V}\): Only \(\mathrm{Zn}\) (\(E^\circ = -0.76\text{ V}\)) satisfies this range. It can displace \(\mathrm{H_2}\) from acid and reduce \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) to \(\mathrm{Cu}\), while being a weaker reducing agent than \(\mathrm{Mg}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Both \(\mathrm{Ag}\) and \(\mathrm{Cu}\) have positive \(E^\circ\) values and cannot displace \(\mathrm{H_2}\) from dilute acid, whereas \(\mathrm{K}\) is stronger than \(\mathrm{Mg}\). Therefore, the correct increasing order is \(\mathrm{Ag} < \mathrm{Cu} < \mathrm{Zn} < \mathrm{Mg} < \mathrm{K}\), and the metal is \(\mathrm{Zn}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_DIAGRAM_Q08 - Zinc-silver galvanic cell potential and notation

questiontext.text:
The galvanic cell diagram below operates based on the reaction \(\mathrm{Zn(s)} + 2\mathrm{Ag^+(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{Ag(s)}\) at \(298\text{ K}\).

What is the standard cell potential (\(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}\)), the direction of electron flow in the external circuit, and the standard cell notation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows a galvanic cell with a \(\mathrm{Zn}\) electrode in \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq)}\) (\(E^\circ = -0.76\text{ V}\)) and an \(\mathrm{Ag}\) electrode in \(\mathrm{Ag^+(aq)}\) (\(E^\circ = +0.80\text{ V}\)) at \(298\text{ K}\). The overall cell reaction is \(\mathrm{Zn(s)} + 2\mathrm{Ag^+(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{Ag(s)}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In standard cell notation, the anode (oxidation half-cell) is written on the left and the cathode (reduction half-cell) on the right, separated by a double vertical line (\(\parallel\)) representing the salt bridge. Electrons flow through the external circuit from the anode to the cathode.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. In the given reaction, \(\mathrm{Zn(s)}\) is oxidised to \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq)}\), so the \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}/Zn}\) half-cell is the anode. \(\mathrm{Ag^+(aq)}\) is reduced to \(\mathrm{Ag(s)}\), so the \(\mathrm{Ag^+/Ag}\) half-cell is the cathode.
2. Calculating the standard cell potential:
\[E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = (+0.80\text{ V}) - (-0.76\text{ V}) = +1.56\text{ V}\]
3. Electrons are released at the \(\mathrm{Zn}\) anode and travel through the external wire to the \(\mathrm{Ag}\) cathode.
4. Writing the cell notation with anode on the left and cathode on the right:
\[\mathrm{Zn(s)} \mid \mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq)} \parallel \mathrm{Ag^+(aq)} \mid \mathrm{Ag(s)}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The positive \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}\) (\(+1.56\text{ V}\)) confirms the reaction is spontaneous as written. Therefore, the standard cell potential is \(+1.56\text{ V}\), electrons flow from \(\mathrm{Zn}\) to \(\mathrm{Ag}\), and the cell notation is \(\mathrm{Zn(s)} \mid \mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq)} \parallel \mathrm{Ag^+(aq)} \mid \mathrm{Ag(s)}\).
